questions.question: A student insists 'present tense = present time,' then meets 'My flight leaves tomorrow.' How do you resolve the contradiction?
questions.solution: Tense is GRAMMAR (verb form); time is MEANING (when it happens) — usually aligned, but timetables, schedules and itineraries use the present simple for FIXED FUTURE events: 'The bus leaves at 6', 'Exams start Monday'. The present tense here signals certainty and schedule, not present time. Rule: present simple + future-time adverbial = scheduled future. The student must separate the two questions: 'what form is the verb?' (present) from 'when does it happen?' (tomorrow).

questions.question: 'The window was broken by him' is grammatically correct, yet teachers mark it down. When is the passive genuinely better than the active — and when is it just hiding the actor?
questions.solution: Use the passive when the RECEIVER matters more than the doer: science reports ('The solution was heated'), unknown agents ('My bike was stolen'), or deliberate tact ('Mistakes were made'). Mark it down when the active is shorter and clearer AND the actor matters — 'He broke the window' beats 'The window was broken by him' because the tacked-on 'by him' proves the doer was the point all along. Test: if your passive needs a long 'by …' phrase, you probably wanted the active voice.

questions.question: Give a foolproof test to never confuse 'its' and 'it's' again, and explain WHY the possessive has no apostrophe.
questions.solution:
Expansion test: if you can replace the word with 'it is' (or 'it has'), write it's; otherwise its. 'The dog wagged its tail' → 'it is tail' is nonsense, so no apostrophe.
Why no apostrophe? Possessive pronouns (his, hers, ours, theirs, its) NEVER take apostrophes — the apostrophe-s ending is reserved for contractions ('can't') and the possessive of NOUNS ('the dog's tail'). 'Its' follows the pronoun family pattern, not the noun pattern. Apostrophes mark omissions and noun-possession only.

questions.question: Direct: 'I will help you tomorrow,' she said. A student reports: 'She said she will help me tomorrow.' Name every shift the student missed and give the correct version.
questions.solution: Three missed shifts: (1) will → would (modal steps back in reported past frames); (2) you → me (pronoun re-anchors to the reporter); (3) tomorrow → the next day (time deictic moves with the reporting moment). Correct: 'She said (that) she would help me the next day.' Principle: reported speech re-centres EVERYTHING — tense, person, place and time — on the reporter, not the original speaker. One unchanged word ('tomorrow') can cost the whole mark because it claims the report was filed the same day.
